body: 68V BTR Holdings, LLC applied to Fairhope's Planning Commission to develop two townhome apartment complexes, Skyline Village and Gables on Lawrence. According to meeting minutes, the commission denied Gables for adverse drainage effects, unmet greenspace requirements, inconsistency with the comprehensive plan and traffic problems, and denied Skyline for drainage, traffic and health, safety and general welfare concerns. 68V sued in federal court in the Southern District of Alabama in 2022. After that court entered summary judgment against 68V on its federal claims and declined to hear its state-law claims, 68V refiled in Baldwin Circuit Court, seeking damages for negligence, invalidation of the denials as arbitrary and capricious, and damages for a deprivation of property without substantive due process under the Alabama Constitution.

The city and commission moved for summary judgment on all three claims, citing municipal immunity, volunteer immunity and substantive immunity. The circuit court denied the motion, and they petitioned the Supreme Court for mandamus on the negligence claim only. Writing the main opinion, Justice Parker reasoned that the claim rested on respondeat superior, so the city and commission could not be liable if their agents were immune. The nine unpaid commissioners were protected by the Volunteer Service Act for negligence, and to the extent 68V alleged bad faith, the opinion said Alabama's municipal-immunity statute also shields agents' bad-faith acts. The planning director, city attorney and mayor, whom 68V faulted for their advice and responses, were protected by substantive immunity because acting on development applications is a public-policy function; the opinion distinguished a 2013 plurality decision that allowed a tort claim on what it called unique facts.

The main opinion called its holding narrow, saying it does not leave planning commissions free to act arbitrarily, does not address 68V's pending claims and does not foreclose a mandamus petition, a remedy 68V chose not to pursue earlier. Justices Wise, Sellers and Cook joined it. Chief Justice Stewart, joined by Justice McCool, and Justices Shaw and Bryan concurred in the result. Justice Mendheim, also concurring in the result, wrote that the negligence claim fails under the municipal-immunity statute alone and that the main opinion's use of substantive immunity deserved more caution, noting that the federal court had found the substantive-immunity arguments lacking when it ruled on a motion to dismiss in 2023.

Justice Mendheim's opinion quoted the federal court's summary of allegations in 68V's federal complaint, including that commission members acknowledged on tape there was no legitimate reason to deny the applications and that the objection was to lower-rent complexes. Those are 68V's allegations, described by the federal court at the motion-to-dismiss stage; the Supreme Court did not resolve them.

timeline.label: 68V sues the City of Fairhope and its Planning Commission in federal court (S.D. Ala. No. 22-0430) over the denied Skyline Village and Gables on Lawrence applications
Federal court rules on the defendants' motion to dismiss, finding their substantive-immunity arguments lacking at that stage
After the federal court rules against 68V on its federal claims, 68V refiles state-law claims in Baldwin Circuit Court (CV-24-900981)
Alabama Supreme Court grants mandamus, holding the City and Planning Commission immune from the negligence claim
